passages.t: As surely as God lives: Job's oath
passages.happening:
‘Job continued his discourse’ (verse 1). “As surely as God lives, who has deprived me of justice” (verse 2), the Almighty who has made his soul bitter, as long as there is breath in him, he swears: “my lips will not speak wickedness, and my tongue will not utter deceit” (verse 4).

“I will never say that you are right; I will maintain my integrity until I die. I will cling to my righteousness and never let go. As long as I live, my conscience will not accuse me” (verses 5-6).

Then he turns to the godless. What hope do they have when God takes their life? Will God hear their cry in distress? “Surely all of you have seen it for yourselves. Why then do you keep up this empty talk?” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The friends have fallen silent. A new opening, literally Job took up his discourse again, marks a fresh start. This is Job's closing statement to them. It is the first of two oaths of innocence in his last speeches; the fuller one comes in chapter 31.

As surely as God lives was the most solemn oath there was. A person who swore by God's life called God to witness the truth of what he said, and to punish him if he lied. Oaths were used in legal disputes when there was no other evidence. Job's case has become exactly that.

There is a paradox here. Job swears by the life of the God who, he says, has denied him justice. Even in protest he appeals to God as the final witness. His complaint is a form of faith, not unbelief.

Integrity, tummah, is the word of the prologue: God pointed to Job's integrity (2:3), and his wife asked whether he still held it (2:9). Here, after all the argument, he says he will keep it until he dies. The breath of God in his nostrils recalls the first man, into whom God breathed the breath of life.
passages.later: The law used such oaths where no other evidence could settle a case: ‘an oath before the LORD shall be made between the parties’ (Exodus 22:11).
passages.hard:
Is Job's refusal to say his friends are right a form of pride?

Some readers hear arrogance in Job's oath. Elihu will accuse him of justifying himself rather than God (32:2), and God will ask whether Job would condemn God to justify himself (40:8). Other readers point out that the book has already told the reader that Job is right about the central point. He did not suffer because of hidden sin, and God himself says so (1:8; 2:3; 42:7). To confess sins he had not committed would have been a lie, and Job refuses to lie even to end his suffering.

Many interpreters hold both views together. Job's integrity is real, and his refusal of the friends' false diagnosis is right. But in defending himself he sometimes speaks as though God were in the wrong, and that is what God challenges at the end. The book does not condemn Job for keeping his innocence. It corrects him for thinking that his innocence gave him the right to judge God.
passages.asks: Job would not lie, even to end his suffering. Ask whether you have ever been pressed to confess to something you did not do, to keep the peace. And ask how you hold on to the truth about yourself without making yourself God's judge.

passages.happening:
“This is the wicked man’s portion from God” (verse 13), the inheritance the ruthless receive. His many sons are destined for the sword, and his survivors will be buried by plague. He may heap up silver like dust and clothes like clay, ‘what he lays up, the righteous will wear, and his silver will be divided by the innocent’ (verse 17).

The house he builds is like a moth's cocoon, like a watchman's hut. He lies down rich and wakes to find everything gone. Terrors overtake him like a flood, and a storm sweeps him away in the night. ‘The east wind carries him away, and he is gone’ (verse 21). It claps its hands at him and hisses him out of his place.
passages.hearers:
This half of the chapter sounds very like the friends. Verse 13 almost exactly repeats the last line of Zophar's second speech (20:29). Many scholars suggest that verses 13 to 23 are Zophar's missing third speech, moved from its place. Others think Job is quoting the friends' teaching back at them, or describing what he wishes on his enemies (verse 7), or saying what he never denied, that God does judge the wicked in the end. Whoever speaks these lines, the book does not deny that God judges. It denies that suffering is always a sign of it.

Fine clothing was a major form of wealth. A watchman's hut was a shelter of branches put up in a field at harvest and abandoned afterward, a picture of something flimsy. The east wind was the hot desert wind, feared for its power. Clapping hands and hissing were gestures of scorn at someone fallen into disaster.
passages.later: Lamentations uses the same gestures of scorn over fallen Jerusalem: ‘All who pass by clap their hands at you in scorn. They hiss and shake their heads at the Daughter of Jerusalem’ (Lamentations 2:15).
passages.asks: The wicked man in this picture built his life on what could be swept away overnight. Ask what you are building on. And ask what would remain if the wind took the rest.
